Before you write  

Ask me any follow-up questions *one round only* to fill unavoidable gaps (e.g., unique mechanism, proof, service area, guarantees, simple testimonial snippets). Keep it to ≤ 5 quick questions.



Research Output (work silently—do *NOT* reveal raw URLs)  

• Bullet summary of industry homepage best practices  

• Top 10 VoC phrases grouped by theme (problem / desire)

7. SOCIAL PROOF SECTION – logos or short testimonial snippets    

8. CTA BLOCK – Button + urgency/benefit line  

9. FAQ – 3 concise Q&As that remove last-minute doubts

You are an expert on AI engineering. I am learning about how to evaluate models to find the best suited one for my application. I will share a note that I took from a book. I want you to improve it and expand it but keeping to that specific topic. The following text is the note: ## Comparative Evaluation
If you want to know which model is the best for you, you can rank models using either *pointwise* evaluation or comparative evaluation.
With pointwise evaluation, you evaluate each model independently, then rank them by their scores.
With comparative evaluation, you evaluate models against each other and compute a ranking from comparison results.
For responses whose quality is subjective, comparative evaluation is typically easier to do than pointwise evaluation. For example, it’s easier to tell which song of the two songs is better than to give each song a concrete score.
However, not all questions should be answered by preference. Many questions should be answered by correctness instead.
When collecting comparative feedback from users, one challenge is to determine what questions can be determined by preference voting and what shouldn’t be.
Comparative evaluation tells us which model is better. It doesn’t tell us how good a model is or whether this model is good enough for our use case.

### Usefulness
There are many benefits to comparative evaluation. 
First, people have found that it’s easier to compare two outputs than to give each output a concrete score. As models become stronger, surpassing human performance, it might become impossible for human evaluators to give model responses concrete scores. However, human evaluators might still be able to detect the difference, and comparative evaluation might remain the only option. 
Second, comparative evaluation aims to capture the quality we care about: human preference.

I attended a chess competition at this high-end and high-ranking all-boys high school as a host—let’s just say it’s School X. After the competition, I watched this flash mob competition with my friends. Before the competition, we noticed this group of students preparing some sort of costume in a hurry in front of the chess venue competition upstairs. After the break when we roamed around, we (and the other competitors) started noticing that some of the school X student is wearing this bizarre "costumes?", one of them looks homeless, as if he had just been robbed. Then we went inside the flash mob competition venue.

At first, there were several pretty decent flash mob groups. I loved this one boys/girls group that utilized some sort of stick or this group that utilizes time stop and re-synchronized their dancing one by one. The School X host had two groups: one was a pretty decent flash mob with this awesome triple backflip move. But then the second group came. The auditorium has this Jumbotron right? Usually it just played the picture of the groups as an introduction. But then it cuts to a live feed of a bunch of students in costumes...? outside on the other side of the school. They then run as fast as they can while making noises to the competition venue.

It was this weird, or unique? A bunch of students (like 35+ instead of the usual 3-7 people). They basically mangled their school uniforms or just wore random outfits. One of them transformed their uniform into a crop top; another had two uniforms mashed together. They had several unique outfits, one of them even wore a motorcycle helmet backward and was somehow still able to see.

I think the best outfit was this combination: headphones worn sideways as a visor-ish thing, plus an earphone, a mask on his head and mouth, Four different kinds of hats, a towel on his chest. Oh and one student wore improvised street cone (yes, the orange street cone) as his pants.

They kinda rotated between each group and had a different theme, so five or seven guys came to the front, danced, went back to the group, then another five came forward, etc. It was... interesting. They obviously hadn’t rehearsed any of the moves at all and only prepared the music remix with a rough outline of the move. It was chaotic but fun as a joke group.

The best part was when the judges commented. Every time the judges gave even the slightest "praise" ("The dance is... unique...?"), the group erupted in happiness. Or when the judges gave any critism ("You guys obviously haven't practiced") they act like they just failed their final exam and breaks down in massive disappointment. It was a good experience. But what do you think of my experience? It was literally once it a lifetime, but apparently, they do this every year?
